_about: Tesla Roadster (2nd gen) research ledger. 'facts' follows pt-maker judged-deck format (id/value/unit/claim/source/checked) plus status/publisher/published/area/slide_use/note. 'qualitative' holds sourced items without a natural number (not read by qa_facts_gate). status: claimed = Tesla/Musk said it; demonstrated = shown live, reported by an outlet; verified = independently measured/confirmed; reported = outlet reporting; Calculated values have no status (the gate allows only the four) and carry basis='calculated'; inputs are named in publisher/note.

facts.claim: Most recent Roadster presentation: the 'Roadster Event', Thursday 2026-10-15 local time (US Central); it was 2026-10-16 in Korea
facts.note: Reuters (via Yahoo Finance) and CNBC date it Thursday Oct 15. YouTube lists it as a past livestream (was_live) uploaded 2026-10-16 UTC.

facts.claim: Scheduled start time, local time at the venue (8:55 pm ET)
facts.note: The X broadcast record lists the scheduled start as 2026-10-16 00:55:00 UTC. Lines up with Tesla's X post 'Roadster event livestream'.

facts.claim: Same start time in Korean time (UTC+9)
facts.publisher: Calculated from event-start-cdt (19:55 CDT, UTC-5) + 14 h
facts.note: Time-zone arithmetic. Consistent with the YouTube release timestamp 2026-10-16 00:55:16 UTC.

facts.claim: Time the liveblog saw the program actually begin (about 5 min after the 20:55 EDT schedule)
facts.note: YouTube's release timestamp is 00:55:16 UTC (on schedule), so the stream was probably up but showed a holding screen first. Minor disagreement.

facts.claim: Length of the official recorded livestream on Tesla's YouTube channel: 1,401 s
facts.note: The Verge: 'The event was less than 30 minutes'. The recording includes music intro/outro.

facts.claim: Venue: SpaceX rocket test and development site, McGregor, Texas (near Waco); stated on stage as 4,000 acres
facts.note: Venue confirmed by Reuters, CNBC and Gizmodo. Some outlets (The Verge, CBC caption) say 'Waco, Texas'; same area.

facts.claim: On stage: Elon Musk (CEO), Franz von Holzhausen (design chief), Lars Moravy (VP vehicle engineering)
facts.note: TechCrunch names Musk and Moravy. BGR liveblog lists all three.

facts.claim: Original event date. Tesla called it off on 2026-09-28, citing weather (show 'can only be held outdoors'), and moved it to 2026-10-15
facts.note: Tesla's X statement: 'we've made the difficult decision to reschedule. New date is October 15.'

facts.claim: View count on Tesla's X post 'Roadster event livestream' at access time
facts.note: Platform counter; it keeps changing. Use with 'as of 2026-10-19'.

facts.claim: View count on the YouTube 'Roadster Event' recording at access time
facts.note: Platform counter; it keeps changing.

facts.claim: Live demo 2: the Roadster jumped over Tesla's lineup (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Semi, Cybercab), twisting in a 'kick flip'
facts.note: TechCrunch lists the same five vehicles. Reuters: 'jump over a truck and other vehicles'.

facts.claim: Four demos were run live: (1) ramp climb, hang upside down, flip and thruster landing; (2) 'kick flip' jump over five Tesla vehicles; (3) 0-60 mph run on the pad; (4) final vertical launch from standstill with a corkscrew rotation and landing
facts.note: Recording times: (1) countdown 00:05:16, 'Well, it worked' 00:07:25; (2) 00:10:35-00:11:30; (3) 00:16:51-00:18:30; (4) 00:21:28-00:22:12. Not counted: the pre-recorded 1 s test clip and the pre-show Raptor engine static fire. Gizmodo lists all four.

facts.unit: min:s into the recording (lift-off; demo segment 21:28-22:12)
facts.claim: Live demo 4 ('let's do the last thing'): the car launched vertically from standstill on its thrusters, rotated in the air and landed; Gizmodo: 'a vertical launch from the ground into a corkscrew'
facts.note: Checked on the Tesla recording (low-resolution frames): lift-off about 00:21:53, landing in a cloud about 00:21:56. BGR liveblog called this part 'precision landings'.

facts.claim: Time Tesla's own timer gave for the live 0-60 mph run: 0.81 s (the run was shown live: q-zero60-run-live; the number is Tesla's)
facts.note: NBC: 'a 0.81-second 0-60 mph time, according to Tesla'. The Verge: 'the company claimed it did so in 0.81 seconds'. Electrek: Tesla 'claimed that the car hit 60mph in 0.81 seconds, after some technical difficulties with the timer'. Livestream 00:18:24-00:18:30. CNBC does not give 0.81 (only 'under a second, according to Tesla's timer'). No independent timing.

facts.claim: A pre-recorded test clip shown on stage put 0-60 mph at about 1 second
facts.note: Gizmodo: 'a clip of the Roadster going from 0 to 60 mph in one second'. Shown on screen, not live.

facts.claim: No person was on board during the stunt demos. Musk: the demo was 'technically autonomous... to make sure we don't kill anyone'
facts.note: Electrek: 'For the demos, nobody was in the car.' CNN: 'The car did not have an actual driver during the demonstration.' E15 (2026-10-19): a 'Starman' mannequin is visible in one car in the livestream (00:09:22-00:09:58, 'that is not a real human'); do not say only a mannequin rode in every demo. Livestream 00:04:24 (autonomous).

facts.claim: Performance trim (road ready, 2 seats, no thrusters): 0-60 mph under 1.6 s
facts.note: Tesla post 01:28 UTC Oct 16: '0-60 Performance (<1.6)'.

facts.claim: Thrust trim (race ready, 2 seats, rear cold-gas thrusters): 0-60 mph under 0.9 s
facts.note: Same post's trim text and Tesla's Roadster page say '<1 second'. Electrek and Not a Tesla App cite 0.85 s from executives.

facts.claim: Rocket trim (air ready, 1 seat, perimeter thrusters, invite only): 0-60 mph under 0.59 s
facts.note: Electrek (Dow) reports that Tesla later gave 0.55 s for the top spec; the one-foot rollout applies to that 0.55 s figure, not to the posted <0.59 s.

facts.claim: Claimed range: over 300 miles
facts.note: Reuters: 'over 300 miles (480 km) on a single charge... less than half of what Musk promised in 2017'.

facts.claim: Rocket trim only: top speed 'up to >230mph (Rocket)' (Tesla's spec post); not a figure for Performance or Thrust
facts.note: On stage Moravy said 'the car can go over 230 miles per hour' without naming a trim (livestream 00:20:23; Reuters). Tesla engineers told Top Gear '214 miles per hour for now' (tg-topspeed-now). Other splits conflict with Tesla's post: TechCrunch (all trims), Electrek Dow (230 Thrust and Rocket, 210 Performance). Always name the trim.

facts.claim: Musk's stated aspiration: 'crack halfway to the speed of sound... Mach .5, maybe a little higher'
facts.note: Livestream 00:20:23. A goal, not a spec.

facts.claim: Seats: two in Performance and Thrust, one in Rocket (the tanks take the second seat)
facts.note: Tesla X post lists the same seat counts.

facts.claim: Three trims: Performance ('By Reservation'), Thrust ('Limited Release'), Rocket ('Invite Only')

facts.unit: L compressed air (about 250 kg), 2 tanks, 10 nozzles
facts.claim: Thruster gas: two carbon-fibre-overwrapped pressure vessels, 600 L total, about 250 kg of air, 10 nozzles
facts.note: TechCrunch and The Verge report the same 600 L / 10 nozzles. Electrek: 200 L in Thrust, plus 400 L in Rocket.

facts.claim: Rear thrusters produce over 80 kN of thrust (exhaust faster than sound, 'Mach diamonds')
facts.note: Gizmodo and Electrek report the same 80 kN.

facts.claim: Thrusters generate 4-5x the force the tires can
The fan suction system under the car 'can pull up to 2 G's', enough to hold the car upside down
facts.note: The Verge reports the same 'up to two Gs of suction force'. Tesla page: holds the car upside down 'even when stationary'.

facts.unit: G cornering (vs 1.26 G typical tire limit)
facts.claim: Fan suction lets the car corner at more than 2 G; tires alone are typically 1.26 G
facts.note: The Drive: 'can pull more than 2.0 lateral Gs'. Not measured.

facts.claim: Downforce figure shown at the event: about 4,700 kg
facts.note: Dow: seems very high for a car under 1,700 kg; 'some liberties may have been taken'.

facts.claim: Refilling the air tanks takes 6-7 hours today; Tesla hopes for 30 minutes
facts.note: Secondary report. Tesla engineers told Top Gear 'two to six hours' for the Thrust trim's 200 L tank (tg-thrust-burst): disputed.

facts.claim: Performance reservation: $50,000, of which $5,000 by card (Tesla: 'fully refundable') and $45,000 by wire within 10 days or the reservation is cancelled
facts.note: Reuters/CBC: Performance needs a $50,000 deposit. Reopened about 2026-09-20 (Electrek). CNBC: deposits taken in the US, Canada and China.

facts.claim: Thrust reservation: $250,000 deposit; Rocket: invite only, no listed deposit
facts.note: TechCrunch reports the same. Payment split for Thrust ($5,000 + $245,000) is reported second-hand only (MotorTrend via search summary): unconfirmed.

facts.claim: Tesla reopened $50,000 Roadster reservations about two weeks before the planned Oct 1 reveal
facts.note: Electrek: reservation is not final until the wire clears.

facts.claim: Musk on stage: production starts in 2028 ('2028, actually', per Electrek). No delivery date given
facts.note: Livestream 00:21:09 (auto-captions: '...production in 2028.' 'Actually' 'actually, for real'). CNBC, NBC and The Verge report the same; no delivery date or price.

facts.unit: mile in the time others do 0.25 mile (claimed)
facts.claim: Musk: 'it is the world's quickest production car 0 to 60. It'll do a half a mile in the time that other cars can do a quarter mile'
facts.note: Not a production car yet; no independent data.

facts.claim: Tesla engineers to Top Gear: top speed is '214 miles per hour for now'; a 330 mph version is being worked on ('It's just gearing')
facts.note: Conflicts with the on-stage '>230 mph'. Wikipedia cites the same Top Gear video.

facts.claim: Tesla engineers to Top Gear: a 330 mph version is planned
facts.note: Goal, not a spec.

facts.unit: MW (about 1,340 hp) base; over 1,000 kW (1,500 hp) Performance and up
facts.claim: Base Roadster: 1 MW (about 1,340 bhp, about 960 lb-ft); Performance and up: over 1,000 kW, '1500 horsepower', from two rear motors on 800-1,000 V
facts.note: Engineers said 'dual motor at the rear axle', not three or four. E19 (2026-10-19): power was claimed (Top Gear 06:26: 'over 1,000 kW ... 1,500 horsepower'; Electrek: 'over 1 MW'); only battery capacity was not disclosed. Status stays claimed.

facts.claim: Two motors, both on the rear axle (rear-wheel drive, torque vectoring)
facts.note: The 2017 prototype was described with three motors and AWD.

facts.claim: Weight target for the lightest version: under 1,700 kg
facts.note: Said as a personal target ('team will kill me for saying this').

facts.claim: Top Gear's recap: 310 to 320 miles of range across the models; Tesla would not confirm battery size
facts.note: Tesla's own post says '>300 miles'.

facts.claim: Engineers: 'hoping to do 15-85 in 10 minutes', pulling over 500 kW from Gen 4 Superchargers
facts.note: Top Gear's recap says 'less than 15 minutes, 15 to 80%'. Treat as a target.

facts.unit: seconds of thrust per fill (Thrust trim, 200 L tank, quarter-mile run)
facts.claim: Thrust trim: one fill of its 200 L air tank gives one charge for a quarter-mile run, thrusting for about five seconds; fill time today two to six hours, hoped under half an hour
facts.note: Top Gear video 22:38-23:07. About straight-line acceleration in the Thrust trim, not about flight or the Rocket trim. Electrek (Dow) reports a 6-7 h fill.

facts.claim: No independent measurement of any 2026 acceleration, speed or range figure was found; the 0.81 s came from Tesla's own timer
facts.note: Verge: 'we'll need to wait for independent testing to confirm'. CNBC: 'according to Tesla's timer'. Electrek (Dow): no independent verification.

facts.unit: ft rollout in Tesla's fastest 0-60 claim
facts.claim: Electrek: 'the 0.55s time includes a one foot rollout' (Tesla's later top-spec figure). This applies to 0.55 s only, not to the posted <0.59 s. Electrek's slow-motion frames show the car still stationary after the thrusters spun up
facts.note: Analysis of Tesla footage, not a measurement.

facts.claim: Tesla shares were up 5% in premarket trading the day after the event; they later fell in a sell-off of AI-linked stocks
facts.note: Later Reuters version via CBC: 'climbed in morning trading on Friday before falling'.

facts.claim: Tesla's Q3 2026 results were due on Oct 21, which analysts said matter more to investors than the reveal
facts.note: eToro's Josh Gilbert quoted by Reuters.

facts.claim: Tesla surprise-unveiled the 2nd-gen Roadster prototype at the end of its Semi truck event in Hawthorne (near Los Angeles), California
facts.note: Also CNBC (2017-11-17 US Eastern) and TechCrunch (2017-11-16). Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim on Tesla's Roadster page: 0-60 mph in 1.9 s
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: 0-100 mph in 4.2 s
facts.note: CNBC reported Musk saying '4 seconds' on stage. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: quarter mile in 8.8 s
facts.note: On stage Musk said 8.9 s (CNBC, NPR, TechCrunch). Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: top speed 'Over 250 mph'
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: 620 miles of range
facts.note: TechCrunch wrote '630 miles of highway'. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim (Musk on stage): 200 kWh battery
facts.note: Not on Tesla's 2017 page. CNBC: 'It will have a 200 kilowatt hour battery pack'. CNBC timestamp 2017-11-17 06:35 UTC (01:35 US Eastern); the URL path says 2017/11/16.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: 10,000 Nm wheel torque
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 claim: four seats (2+2), all-wheel drive
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 base price: $200,000 (no 2026 price announced)
facts.note: Reuters 2026: 'Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000'. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 Founders Series price: $250,000, paid in full up front; 1,000 cars. (As of 2026, $250,000 is the Thrust trim's reservation and no price has been announced.)
facts.note: CNBC 2017-11-17: 'Those who want to buy one of the 1,000 Founders Series Roadsters will have to shell out $250,000 upfront.' Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2017 base reservation: $50,000; $5,000 at once and at least $50,000 in total within 10 days
facts.note: Payment split per NPR 2017-11-17. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: In 2017 Tesla said the Roadster was expected to be available in 2020
facts.note: CNBC: 'The car is expected to be available in 2020.' Reuters 2026: Musk 'said that deliveries would begin in 2020'. CNBC date is 2017-11-17 US Eastern (URL path says 2017/11/16).

facts.claim: Musk, 2018-06-09: 'SpaceX option package... ~10 small rocket thrusters... Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly'
facts.note: Primary post read via api.fxtwitter.com; CNBC 2026-10-15 quotes it.

facts.claim: 2020-07-22 Q2 earnings call: Roadster among products for 'the next 12 to 18 months' (mid-2021 to early 2022)
facts.note: Electrek's 2026 recap says 'July 2020: pushed to 2021'; in May 2020 Electrek had read a Rogan remark as 2022. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2021-01-28, Musk: 'Finishing engineering this year, production starts next year'
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2021-09-01, Musk: 'Assuming 2022 is not mega drama, new Roadster should ship in 2023'
facts.note: TechCrunch 2021-09-02 reports the same. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: Tesla removed the $200,000 price and Founders Series from its Roadster page in late 2021 (present on 2021-12-09 snapshot, gone by 2022-01-20)
facts.note: Electrek dates it 'between November 13 and December 12'. Whether Founders sold out is unconfirmed. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2023-05-16 shareholder meeting, Musk: '...hopefully – this is not a commitment – start production next year'
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.unit: ship year (claimed); demo by end of 2024
facts.claim: 2024-02-28, Musk: 'radically increased the design goals'; production design unveiled by end of 2024, 'aiming to ship next year'
facts.note: Reuters (via BusinessToday) reported the same. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: Musk, 2024-02-28: '0-60mph < 1 sec. And that is the least interesting part'
facts.note: Primary post read via api.fxtwitter.com. The Drive (2024-02-28) was skeptical ('Sure, Whatever').

facts.claim: 2025-10-31 (Joe Rogan podcast): Musk said Tesla was getting close to demonstrating the prototype, an 'unforgettable' demo; reported as targeted before end of 2025
facts.note: 'Before the end of the year' is the reporter's summary; exact wording unconfirmed. CNBC 2026: Musk hoped for a demo before end of 2025; it did not happen. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: Electrek's timeline: 'November 2025: Production moved to 2027 or 2028'
facts.note: E17 (2026-10-19): source changed from TechCrunch. TechCrunch 2025-11-06 reports production 12-18 months after an April 2026 unveil, which supports 2027 only; Electrek 2026-10-13 states '2027 or 2028'. This is slip 6 of Electrek's 'at least six production slips'. Demo date: demo-promise-2025-11. Re-read 2026-10-19.

facts.claim: 2025-11-06 shareholder meeting, Musk: 'that demo event will be April 1 of next year'; he said April 1 gives him 'deniability'
facts.note: Electrek 2025-11-06 and 2026-09-12 report the same. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2026-03-17, Musk on X: new Roadster unveil 'probably in late April'
facts.note: Wording differs between sources. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: Q1 2026 earnings call (2026-04-21), Musk: 'We may be able to debut that in a month or so'
facts.note: Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: The Information (via Electrek): Roadster demo slipped to August or later, tied to SpaceX thruster work
facts.note: Four people familiar, per The Information. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.claim: 2026-09-12: Tesla teaser 'Go for launch' with '10.01' set the reveal for October 1
Electrek's count before the event: at least six production slips since the 2020 promise (the last one is the 2025-11 move to 2027 or 2028)
facts.note: E18 (2026-10-19): a production count, separate from unveil-dates-count (7 unveil dates). Electrek's list, one ledger id each: 1 delay-2020-07 (2021), 2 delay-2021-01 (2022), 3 delay-2021-09 (2023), 4 delay-2023-05 (2024), 5 delay-2024-02 (2025), 6 delay-2025-11 (2027 or 2028). The 2028 stated at the 2026-10-15 event (production-2028) is the new promise, not one of the six. Author holds Roadster referral awards (disclosed).

facts.claim: Electrek's count before the event (2026-10-13): seven unveil/demo dates; 7 dates means 6 changes, not 7

facts.unit: years between promised (2020) and newly claimed (2028) production
facts.claim: Gap between the 2017 promise (2020) and the 2026 claim (2028): 8 years
facts.note: 2028 - 2020 = 8. Both inputs are Tesla claims; show the two years next to the number.

facts.claim: Time from the 2017 prototype unveil to the 2026 event: 3,255 days (about 8.9 years)
facts.note: Plain date arithmetic; show both dates next to the number.

facts.claim: TechRadar: in March 2025 Tesla's US site still asked $5,000 plus $45,000 within 10 days for a Roadster reservation
facts.note: Teslarati (2026-09-21) instead says reservations were paused from 2021: disputed. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.unit: USD initially kept on a cancelled reservation
facts.claim: Marques Brownlee's cancelled 2017 reservation: Tesla first returned $45,000 and kept $5,000, later refunded it
facts.note: Sam Altman also publicised refund trouble (TechCrunch 2025-11-01); Musk said he was refunded within 24 h. Opened by the research sub-agent.

facts.unit: s (0-60 mph, measured, 1-ft rollout, prepped surface)
facts.claim: Tesla Model S Plaid: MotorTrend measured 0-60 mph in 1.98 s on a prepped (VHT) surface, 2.07 s on normal pavement; Tesla claimed 1.99 s
facts.note: Independent measurement under Tesla-chosen conditions. NBC 2026: the 0.81 s demo is more than a second faster than the Plaid. Opened by the research sub-agent. E20 (2026-10-19): the unit already holds the condition (1-ft rollout, prepped surface); show it wherever rollout is discussed.

facts.unit: s (0-60 mph, as stated by The Verge)
facts.claim: The Verge: 'the McMurtry Spéirling single-seater holds the record for quickest acceleration from 0 to 60mph in 1.35 seconds'
facts.note: Exact sentence re-read 2026-10-19. The Verge names no test; its link goes to McMurtry's upside-down-driving page. Other public values differ: 1.4 s measured by Carwow (cmp-mcmurtry-0-60-carwow); the fact-check also found 1.38 s and 1.55 s (not checked here). Disputed: for a chart bar use cmp-mcmurtry-0-60-carwow or drop McMurtry.

facts.unit: s (0-60 mph, measured by Carwow, prototype, Silverstone)
facts.claim: Carwow measured the McMurtry Spéirling prototype at 0-60 mph in 1.4 s on a freshly dried Silverstone circuit (Motor1: 'CarWow clocks an astonishing 0-60 mph (96 kph) time of 1.4 seconds')
facts.note: Independent media measurement of a prototype, second run. Rollout not stated by Motor1 (search summaries say Motor Authority reported no rollout; not opened, 403).

facts.unit: s (0-60 mph, 1-ft rollout, non-prepped asphalt, independently verified by Dewesoft and Racelogic)
facts.claim: Rimac Nevera: 0-60 mph in 1.74 s in a 2023 record session, 'independently verified by Dewesoft and RaceLogic', with a standard one-foot rollout on non-prepped asphalt (official spec 1.85 s)
facts.publisher: Rimac newsroom (records verified by Dewesoft and Racelogic)
facts.note: E14 (2026-10-19): E11 was wrong; the press release says the records were 'independently verified by Dewesoft and RaceLogic', both with on-site teams; both loggers show 1.74 s. Motor Authority reports the same. The Drive (2024-02-28) cites it as the production-car record. Re-read 2026-10-19.

facts.claim: A Swiss student-built electric car with a vacuum (fan) system hit 60 mph in 0.956 s; it weighed 309 lb
facts.note: Shows sub-1-second is physically possible for a tiny fan car; not a road car.

facts.claim: Rimac Nevera's top-speed record: 268 mph
facts.note: Context only.

facts.claim: BYD Yangwang U9 Xtreme reached 308 mph in testing
facts.note: Context only.

facts.claim: Musk's 'halfway to the speed of sound' goal is about 383 mph, over 150 mph above the announced top speed
facts.note: Goal, not a spec.

facts.claim: 60 mph is about 97 km/h (Reuters writes 'zero to 60 mph (97 kph)')
facts.note: Use when saying '0-60 mph' to a Korean audience: 시속 0→97 km.

facts.claim: Claimed 2026 range in km: over 480 km
facts.note: Reuters: 'over 300 miles (480 km)'.

facts.claim: Claimed 2026 top speed in km/h, Rocket trim only: over 370 km/h
facts.note: Reuters: 'over 230 mph (370 kph)'.

facts.claim: 2017 range claim in km: 620 miles is about 998 km
facts.note: Top Gear and Wikipedia round it to 1,000 km.

facts.claim: 2017 top-speed claim in km/h: 250 mph is about 402 km/h

qualitative.claim: Live demo 1: an unoccupied Roadster climbed a curved multi-storey ramp, clung to it upside down with fan suction, launched off, flipped, and landed on its wheels with cold-gas thrusters
qualitative.note: Also described by CNBC, CNN, NBC, The Verge, The Drive. Suction figure: see suction-2g-2026.

qualitative.claim: Tesla said it plans a follow-on demo: another attempt at Evel Knievel's Snake River Canyon jump
qualitative.note: Livestream 00:19:58. TechCrunch: Musk said Tesla may try it.

qualitative.claim: "Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date."
qualitative.note: Neutral framing line for the history slide.

qualitative.claim: "It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers" (Gene Munster, Deepwater Asset Management, on X)
"It's completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold." (Andrew J. Hawkins)
"The engineering here is real." (Fred Lambert, who holds Roadster reservations)
"We're not talking about sustained flight. We are literally talking about hopping." (Roger Connor, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, before the event)
qualitative.note: Said before the event; CNN: true flight 'remains to be proven'.

qualitative.claim: Stunts were seen in person by a live crowd of fans and investors; Musk: 'we need an audience to prove that it's not AI'
qualitative.note: Reuters quotes Sawyer Merritt: 'I just saw this in person'.

qualitative.claim: No long-range or sustained flight was shown; only short hops, flips and landings
qualitative.note: CNN: 'It certainly didn't have any demonstration of long-range flight.'

qualitative.claim: Different cars were used for each demo, which suggests the thrusters run only a few seconds at full power
No reports found of attendees, journalists or customers riding in or driving the 2026 car
qualitative.note: Absence of evidence, not proof. On stage, Franz said 'two guys got out of' the display car (00:13:47).

qualitative.claim: Tesla's page: Rocket 'Not approved for public road use'; 'not available in all regions'. Musk on street use: 'Depends on your street'
qualitative.note: Georgetown law professor David Vladeck (Reuters via CBC): 'There is going to be a long process to let anything like that on a road.'

qualitative.claim: Tesla on Rocket: 'So...yes, it can fly'
qualitative.note: Flight shown = short powered hops; no certification mentioned.

qualitative.claim: Musk: long-term the Roadster will be 'the only manually driven car that Tesla makes'; no FSD
qualitative.note: CNBC: Tesla left FSD out of the Roadster.

qualitative.claim: Tesla: design inspired by the SR-71 and F-35; 'Cyber' design language
No price and no delivery date for any trim were given at the event
A 0-60 mph run with the rear thrusters was performed live on the test pad in front of the audience; the time on Tesla's timer is in demo-zero60-live (claimed)
qualitative.note: CNBC: 'a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience'. NBC: 'Minutes later, it sped away'. Livestream 00:16:51-00:18:30.
